title: Documents You Need for Business Funding
seo_title: Documents Needed for Business Funding | Fidelity Funding
meta_description: A complete checklist of documents needed for business funding, from bank statements and ID to tax returns, financials and extras for equipment or real estate.
dek: Having the right paperwork ready is the single easiest way to shorten the path from application to decision.
intro: Ask anyone who has applied for business funding what slowed them down and the answer is rarely the underwriting itself. It is the hunt for a missing page of a statement, a driver's license that expired last spring, or a tax return the accountant has not sent yet.

The list of documents varies a lot by product. A fast working-capital option might need little more than recent bank statements and an application, while an SBA loan can require a thick folder. Below is a complete checklist, grouped by how often each item is requested, so you can gather what you can in an afternoon and know what to expect for the rest.

sections.h2: The core set almost every funder asks for
paragraphs: These are the items to gather first because they come up for nearly every product. Having them in a single folder, scanned clearly, is worth more than any trick for speeding up a review.

Keep files in PDF where possible, name them plainly, and make sure every page is present. Cropped screenshots and missing last pages are the most common reason a file bounces back for a second request.
bullets: A completed application, signed by an owner
Government-issued photo ID for each owner, current and legible
Three to six months of recent business bank statements, every page
A voided check or bank letter confirming account details
Business name, EIN, address and start date matching your records
Processing statements if you accept cards, often the last three to six months

sections.h2: Bank and processing statements: what makes them usable
paragraphs: Download statements directly from your bank instead of photographing a printout. Complete PDFs show account numbers, balances and every transaction, and reviewers can read them quickly. If you use more than one operating account, submit each and label them so transfers can be matched.

For card-accepting businesses, merchant processing statements help show sales volume and mix. If you are unsure what yours say or whether you are paying more than you should, Fidelity Funding's card-processing partner, PayPilot by MCCPS, offers a statement review at no pressure, which can be useful to do while you are gathering paperwork anyway.

Statements also reveal timing. If your deposits cluster around the first and fifteenth because of how clients pay, a reviewer will see that pattern at a glance. A short note explaining your billing cycle can turn a lumpy month into an understood one.

Funders need to confirm who the business is and who owns it. Depending on your structure, expect to produce some of the following. Names must be consistent across them, so if your articles say 'Harbor Mechanical LLC' and your bank account says 'Harbor Mech.', fix or explain it before submitting.
bullets: Articles of organization or incorporation, and any amendments
Operating agreement or corporate bylaws showing ownership percentages
EIN confirmation letter from the IRS
Business licenses or professional licenses your industry requires
Commercial lease, or proof of ownership of your location
DBA registration if you operate under a trade name

sections.h2: Tax and financial documents for larger or slower products
paragraphs: Traditional loans and many SBA programs ask for more history. Typical requests include the last two or three years of business tax returns, the owner's personal returns, a current year-to-date profit and loss statement, a balance sheet, and sometimes a debt schedule listing existing loans with balances, payments and lenders.

If you do not keep formal financials, a bookkeeper can usually produce a profit and loss from your accounting software in a day or two. Ask your CPA to confirm what they are comfortable sharing, and to flag anything that needs explaining, such as a one-time loss or a change in ownership.

Some funding types add their own paperwork. Equipment financing usually needs a vendor quote or invoice describing the asset. Invoice factoring needs an accounts-receivable aging report and copies of the invoices being financed. Real estate-related requests may need a purchase contract, appraisal and insurance details. Construction and contracting businesses are often asked for signed contracts, change orders or a work-in-progress schedule.

If you have liens, judgments, a past bankruptcy or open disputes, have the paperwork ready: releases, payment plans, or discharge documents. Raising them yourself and showing resolution reads far better than letting an underwriter discover them.

sections.h2: How to organize it and where Fidelity Funding fits
paragraphs: Build one folder with subfolders for banking, legal, tax and financial, and add a short cover note describing the business, what you need the funds for and any unusual items in the statements. A tidy submission signals an organized owner, which tends to help.

Fidelity Funding's application is short, and a funding specialist reviews your options with you, including which documents the different funding partners are likely to want. You can often start with just the core set and add more only if a partner asks. Requirements vary by funding partner and underwriting, and gathering documents does not guarantee an approval, but it does remove the most common source of delay.
steps: Download the last four to six months of statements for every business account.
Photograph or scan IDs for all owners at readable resolution.
Collect formation documents and the EIN letter into one folder.
Request year-to-date financials and last year's returns from your bookkeeper or CPA.
Write a short note listing odd deposits, large withdrawals and any open liens.

key_takeaways: Bank statements, owner ID, an application and a voided check form the core set for most products.
Complete, unedited PDF statements prevent the most common delays.
Tax returns and financials matter more for loans and SBA programs than for fast working capital.
Equipment, factoring and contract work each add their own paperwork.
Requirements vary by funding partner and underwriting, so ask a specialist what applies to you.

faq.q: What is the minimum I need to start applying?
faq.a: Usually a short application, owner ID and recent business bank statements. Fidelity Funding's initial review uses a soft credit pull, so you can begin with that core set and a specialist will tell you if a funding partner needs anything more. Requirements vary by partner and product, and are not guaranteed to be identical for every business.

faq.q: Do I need tax returns for working capital funding?
faq.a: Not always. Many alternative working-capital products rely mainly on bank statements and revenue. Larger loans, SBA programs and some lines of credit commonly ask for business and personal tax returns. Having the last two years available saves time if a funding partner asks.

faq.q: What if my business is new and has no tax returns?
faq.a: Funders can often work from recent bank statements, a business plan, projections or the owner's personal documents. Expect scrutiny on time in business and deposits. Options may be more limited and terms vary by funding partner and underwriting.

faq.q: Why do funders want every page of my statements?
faq.a: Missing pages hide transactions and balances, and a reviewer cannot verify revenue from fragments. Altered or cropped pages can also raise fraud concerns. Download full statements directly from your bank to avoid delays and questions.

Yes, most funders accept secure uploads or email of PDFs. Use clear scans, avoid photos taken at an angle, and send sensitive items such as IDs and statements only through the channel your specialist provides.
